aspects.says: Double-checked locking needs a volatile field, a second check under the lock, and no lock once the value exists.
final fields, including record components, are visible to every thread once construction completes, as long as this did not escape.
Without volatile or synchronization a thread may never see another thread's write, because the JIT may hoist a flag read out of a loop.
aspects.reason: practised on 5.1.4 by 'A stop flag the JIT cannot hoist', whose edge case is exactly a non-volatile flag

aspects.says: volatile, synchronized, Thread.start and Thread.join each create a happens-before edge that guarantees visibility.
aspects.reason: the happens-before rules are the subject of module 18 (5.2.x), whose pages practise them; this page restates them as a summary table

aspects.says: The Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom gives a lazy, thread-safe singleton with no lock and no volatile, through class initialization.
A visibility bug may not show in interpreted mode and appear only after the JIT compiles the code, so passing tests prove nothing.
basis: section:1. JIT compiler hoisting and the -Xint flag

aspects.says: Plain long and double reads and writes may tear on 32-bit JVMs, and volatile makes them atomic.
basis: section:3. 64-bit value tearing for long and double

aspects.says: The piggyback works only in its order: the plain writes come before the volatile write, and a reader reads the volatile variable before the plain fields.
aspects.reason: a wrong order shows only when a reader runs between two writes inside one publish call, an interleaving no test can force without a hook inside the method; 'Publish a report behind one volatile flag' grades the volatile flag and gives the order as the page's advice

aspects.says: Plain writes made before a volatile write are visible to any thread that later reads that volatile variable.
synchronized gives visibility only between threads that lock the same monitor, so readers and writers must share one lock.
basis: section:5. Forgetting that synchronized visibility applies only to the same monitor

aspects.says: synchronized gives both mutual exclusion and visibility, which a compound update of shared state needs.
Publishing this from a constructor, for example by registering a listener, lets others see the object before its fields are set.
basis: section:2. Final fields and the `this` escape problem

aspects.says: A reference published without synchronization can expose an object whose fields still hold their default values.
basis: section:4. Unsafe publication of mutable objects

aspects.says: VarHandle offers finer memory-ordering modes, such as acquire and release, for advanced cases.
basis: section:Evolution of Visibility Mechanisms Across Java Versions
aspects.reason: named as an advanced option only; the page shows no VarHandle code to practise

aspects.says: Virtual threads do not change the visibility rules; the same JMM guarantees apply.
aspects.reason: a statement that nothing changes, so there is nothing new to check; virtual-thread pinning is asked about on 5.3.4

aspects.says: volatile is enough for state that is only read or written, such as a stop flag, and is cheaper than synchronized.
aspects.reason: practised on 5.1.4 by 'A stop flag the JIT cannot hoist', a flag that is only read and written

aspects.says: volatile does not make a read-modify-write such as count++ atomic; an atomic class or synchronized does.
basis: section:2. Volatile does NOT provide atomicity for compound operations
aspects.reason: lost updates on read-modify-write are the subject of lesson 5.3.2 (atomicity violations), whose practices check them; a lost update cannot be forced deterministically on this page's plain counter
